extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency lawyers, judges, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the role of notice-and-comment procedures and the circumstances under which agencies may invoke the APA's good cause exception, including effects on deliberation, democratic legitimacy, and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of comments on final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unclear how much comments influence final rules that agencies ultimately adopt; agencies frequently seem to have their minds set on the substantive fundamentals of rules by the time they specify a proposed rule in a NOPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies find agencies may make some changes requested by commenters but 'rarely alter the heart of the proposal.' The lack of effect reflects (a) limited effective public participation and (b) extensive pre-NOPR consultations. Even when comments do not change the rule, notice-and-comment may still reinforce incentives created by judicial review to consider data and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for effective commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: To comment effectively, one must be aware that a rule has been proposed, have the incentive to comment, and have relevant information about how the rule will operate that goes beyond mere preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most individuals affected by a rule rarely satisfy these three prerequisites. Effective comments therefore tend to require knowledge of the rulemaking, motivation to invest time, and substantive information about impacts and plausible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance of interest groups and focused interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Most comments are filed by interest groups representing significant stakeholders; focused interests (with a smaller number of members each with substantial stakes) have an advantage over groups with diffuse interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show a high proportion of comments come from companies, trade associations, unions, governments, and public-interest groups. Business and industry groups often file the majority of comments because they can justify the costs of preparing meaningful submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-NOPR consultation reduces comment impact
rubrics_metrics.description: By the time a rule is proposed (NOPR), agency staff often has discussed the proposal with significant interest groups and already knows most of the information the comments subsequently provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The timing of rulemaking concentrates decisionmaking in the pre-notice period; agencies use pre-NOPR interactions to ascertain stakeholder views. Where agencies rely heavily on pre-NOPR consultations, comments are less likely to directly prompt changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-look reasoned decisionmaking requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the reasoned decisionmaking standard, courts review the agency’s reasons: agencies must 'examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation... including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made,' must not rely on improper factors, must consider important aspects of the problem, and must avoid implausible explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether the agency addressed data raised in comments, considered alternatives, and provided adequate explanations. Failure to respond to significant comments or to consider important alternatives can render a rule arbitrary and capricious (see Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm and cited circuit cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments primarily create a record for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment proceedings serve to create a record for judicial review rather than solely to secure public input to persuade the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'threat' of judicial review encourages agencies to vet proposals and to gather and consider matters likely to be raised by comments. Empirical work shows comments are more likely to prompt changes when agencies have not already engaged in extensive pre-NOPR stakeholder discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments as imperfect indicator of democratic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenting requires investment and knowledge; the willingness to incur these costs may signal the value commenters place on an outcome, but participation is biased toward focused interests and many individual commenters lack technical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic rulemaking lowers filing costs and increases participation, but increased volume does not necessarily make the process more democratic because of representativeness and comprehension issues. Thus notice-and-comment should be seen more as an accountability/transparency mechanism than as reliably capturing public preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges from mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments pose difficult challenges for agencies trying to extract information about public preferences; agencies must separate bot and malattributed comments from those genuinely submitted by people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many identical or mass-submitted comments appear, agencies face questions about representativeness and the role of intermediary groups that orchestrate campaigns. Agencies should develop techniques to distinguish genuine individualized input from mass or automated submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments function as a 'fire alarm' to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments can alert members of Congress to stakeholder concerns about a rule (either because constituents are affected or because organized groups mobilize), generating political pressure that may lead Congress to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While congressional reversals of rules are rare, a groundswell of strongly worded opposition in comments can spur congressional attention and possible intervention (examples include use of Congressional Review Act and historical reversals). Agencies should recognize political signaling as a practical effect of comment activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit calculus for invoking the good cause exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal advantage of invoking the good cause exception is speed: it allows an agency to adopt and implement rules more quickly than notice-and-comment, which is beneficial to the extent the rule is better than the status quo; the greater the rule's impact, the greater the benefit of reducing delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, delay alone was insufficient to justify good cause except where delay would cause imminent harm; courts and commentators consider the expected public costs and benefits of faster implementation. For low-impact rules, direct final rulemaking or proceeding with comments may be preferable because procedural costs are typically small relative to regulatory stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial oversight shapes agency organizational responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The prospect of judicial review (hard-look) has led agencies to hire experts, staff to review/respond to comments, economists, and lawyers to prepare preambles and defend rules, thereby influencing agency deliberative practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological literature on accountability suggests that review by an external reviewer with unknown views encourages more thorough agency deliberation. Agencies develop techniques to promote discussion and to build records for judicial review; however, this can also institutionalize certain forms of expertise and responsiveness to particular constituencies.
